rooms.about: This year you will read stories, poems, plays and nonfiction closely, explain what they mean using details, grow your vocabulary, and write strong opinion, informative and narrative pieces.

learn: Good readers do more than read the words. They stop, think and ask questions like: What is happening? Why did the character do that? What does the author want me to notice?
When you answer a question about a text, you need evidence. Evidence is a detail from the text that proves your answer. You can quote the exact words or put them in your own words.

An inference is a smart guess that uses clues from the text plus what you already know. If a character slams a door and stomps away, you can infer she is angry, even if the author never says the word angry.
A helpful sentence frame is: I think ___ because the text says ___. This shows your idea and the proof together.
units.try: Read this: Maya peeked out the window for the tenth time. She checked the clock, then ran to the door at every sound. What can you infer about Maya? Write one sentence using the frame: I think ___ because the text says ___. (Sample: I think Maya is waiting for someone because the text says she checked the clock and ran to the door at every sound.)
check: A smart guess using text clues and what you know
A word the author made up
A detail from the text that supports your answer
Your favorite part of the book
A picture you draw after reading

learn: The theme is the big lesson or message of a story. It is usually not stated directly. Themes are often about life, such as: honesty matters, or true friends help each other.
To find the theme, look at how the main character changes and what they learn by the end. Ask: What does the author want readers to understand about life?

A summary tells the most important events in order, in your own words. It is short. It includes the main character, the problem, key events and how the problem is solved, but not every small detail or your opinion.
units.try: Think of the fable of the tortoise and the hare. Write a three-sentence summary: who, the problem, how it ends. Then write the theme in one sentence. (Sample theme: Slow and steady effort can beat speed and showing off.)
check: What is the theme of a story?
The lesson or message about life
The place where the story happens
What should a summary leave out?

learn: Characters are the people or animals in a story. We learn about them through what they say, do, think and how others treat them. These are called character traits, such as brave, selfish or curious.
The setting is where and when the story happens. A setting can change how characters act. A storm at sea creates danger; a quiet library calls for whispering.
The plot is the order of events. Most plots have a beginning, a problem or conflict, rising action, a climax (the most exciting part), and a resolution where the problem is solved.
When you describe a character, give a trait and a detail that proves it. Example: Leo is generous because he shares his lunch with a new student.
units.try: Choose a character from a book you know. Write two traits for that character and one action from the story that proves each trait.
check: What is the climax of a story?

learn: Stories (prose) are written in sentences and paragraphs. Poems are written in lines and stanzas. A stanza is a group of lines, like a paragraph in a poem.
Poems often use rhythm (a beat), rhyme (words with the same ending sound) and meter (a pattern of strong and weak syllables). Some poems, called free verse, do not rhyme at all.
Plays, also called dramas, are written to be performed. They have a cast of characters, dialogue (the words characters say) and stage directions in parentheses that tell actors how to move or speak.
Plays are divided into acts and scenes, the way a book is divided into chapters.
units.try: Turn this sentence into two lines of a play: Sam whispered to Ana that he had found the lost key. Write the character name, a colon, the words, and a stage direction in parentheses. (Sample: SAM: (whispering) Ana, I found the key!)
check: A group of lines in a poem
A line spoken by an actor
How actors should move or speak

learn: Point of view is who is telling the story. In first person, the narrator is a character in the story and uses words like I, me and we.
In third person, the narrator is outside the story and uses words like he, she and they. A third-person narrator may know the thoughts of one character or of many characters.
Point of view changes what readers know. A first-person narrator only knows his or her own thoughts, so readers might not learn what other characters are feeling.
To compare points of view, ask: How would this story be different if another character told it?
units.try: Read: I dropped my tray and everyone turned to stare. My face felt hot. Rewrite these two sentences in third person, using the name Jordan. (Sample: Jordan dropped his tray and everyone turned to stare. His face felt hot.)
check: Which words signal first-person point of view?
In third person, the narrator is…

units.t: Main Idea and Text Structure in Nonfiction
learn: Nonfiction texts give true information. The main idea is what the whole text or paragraph is mostly about. Supporting details are facts, examples and numbers that explain the main idea.

Authors organize nonfiction in different structures. Chronological order tells events in time order. Compare and contrast shows how things are alike and different. Cause and effect explains why something happens.
Problem and solution describes a problem and how it was or could be solved. Description gives many details about one topic.
Text features help you find information: headings, captions, bold words, diagrams, charts, a glossary and an index.
units.try: Read: Beavers build dams across streams. The dams block the water and form ponds. These ponds give homes to fish, frogs and birds. What is the text structure? (Answer: cause and effect. The dam causes a pond, and the pond causes new homes for animals.)
check: What a text is mostly about
The longest word in the text
A text telling events in time order uses which structure?

learn: Many words are built from parts. A prefix comes at the beginning and changes meaning: un- and dis- mean not, re- means again, pre- means before, mis- means wrongly.
A suffix comes at the end: -ful means full of, -less means without, -er can mean one who, -able means can be. So careless means without care, and readable means can be read.
Greek and Latin roots also help. Tele means far, graph means write, port means carry, and aud means hear. A telegraph sends writing far away.
Context clues are hints in nearby sentences. A writer may give a definition, a synonym, an example or an opposite to help you figure out a hard word.
units.try: Use word parts to define these words: rewrite, hopeless, preview, portable. (Answers: write again; without hope; see before; able to be carried.)
check: What does the prefix re- mean?

learn: Figurative language uses words in a creative way that is not meant literally. It helps readers picture things and feel more.
A simile compares two things using like or as: Her smile was as bright as the sun. A metaphor compares without like or as: The classroom was a zoo.
Personification gives human actions to things that are not human: The wind whispered through the trees. Hyperbole is a big exaggeration: I have told you a million times.
An idiom is a saying whose meaning is different from its words. It's raining cats and dogs means it is raining very hard. Break a leg means good luck.
units.try: Write one simile and one metaphor about a thunderstorm. (Samples: The thunder boomed like a giant drum. The lightning was a silver crack in the sky.)
check: He ran as fast as a cheetah
What does the idiom 'piece of cake' mean?

learn: Relative pronouns connect ideas: who, whose, whom, which and that. Example: The girl who won the race is my cousin.
Progressive verb tenses show ongoing action using a form of be plus -ing: I was walking (past), I am walking (present), I will be walking (future).

Modal verbs like can, may, must, should and might show ability, permission or how likely something is. A prepositional phrase begins with a word like in, on, under or after and ends with a noun: under the bridge.
Use a comma before and, but or so when joining two complete sentences. Use quotation marks around a speaker's exact words and capitalize proper nouns, like names and places.
units.try: Fix this sentence: we was going to the park but it started to rain. (Answer: We were going to the park, but it started to rain.)
check: Which sentence uses the past progressive tense?
Which word is a relative pronoun?

units.t: The Writing Process and Types of Writing
learn: Writers use the writing process: prewrite (plan), draft (write it out), revise (improve the ideas), edit (fix spelling, capitals and punctuation) and publish (share a final copy). Strong paragraphs have a topic sentence, details and a closing sentence.

Opinion writing states what you think and supports it with reasons and facts. Begin with your opinion, give at least three reasons with details, use linking words like because and for example, and end with a conclusion.
Informative writing teaches about a topic using facts grouped into paragraphs. Narrative writing tells a story, real or imagined, with a clear order of events, dialogue and sensory details.
For research, gather facts from more than one trusted source, take notes in your own words, and list the sources you used.
units.try: Plan an opinion piece: Should students have recess every day? Write your opinion, then three reasons with transition words like first, also and finally. (Sample reasons: exercise helps the body, breaks help us focus, and recess builds friendships.) Then reread once to revise and once to edit.
check: Which step of the writing process fixes spelling and punctuation?

rooms.about: Grade 4 builds place value to one million, multi-digit multiplication and division, fractions and decimals, measurement, and the geometry of lines and angles.

units.t: Place Value to One Million and Rounding
learn: Each place in a number is worth 10 times the place to its right. The places are ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, hundred thousands and millions. In 345,812 the 4 is in the ten thousands place, so it is worth 40,000.
Numbers can be written three ways. Standard form: 345,812. Expanded form: 300,000 + 40,000 + 5,000 + 800 + 10 + 2. Word form: three hundred forty-five thousand, eight hundred twelve.
To compare numbers, line up the places and compare from the left. Use > (greater than), < (less than) or =.
To round, look at the digit to the right of the rounding place. If it is 5 or more, round up. If it is 4 or less, keep the digit the same. Then change the digits to the right to zeros.
units.try: Round 47,682 to the nearest thousand. Step 1: The thousands digit is 7. Step 2: Look right at the hundreds digit, 6. Step 3: 6 is 5 or more, so round up: 7 becomes 8. Step 4: Zeros after: 48,000.
check: What is the value of the 6 in 268,415?
What is 52,349 rounded to the nearest hundred?

learn: To add multi-digit numbers, line up the digits by place value. Start with the ones and move left. If a column adds to 10 or more, regroup (carry) the extra ten to the next place.
To subtract, also start with the ones. If the top digit is smaller, regroup (borrow) 1 from the next place to the left, which gives 10 more to the place you are working on.
Check subtraction by adding: the answer plus the number you subtracted should equal the starting number.
Estimate first by rounding. If your exact answer is far from your estimate, check your work.
units.try: Find 6,204 − 2,817. Ones: 4 − 7 needs regrouping. Borrow from tens, but tens is 0, so borrow from hundreds: 2 hundreds becomes 1, tens become 10, then 9, ones become 14. 14 − 7 = 7. 9 − 1 = 8. 1 − 8 needs regrouping: 11 − 8 = 3, thousands 5. 5 − 2 = 3. Answer: 3,387. Check: 3,387 + 2,817 = 6,204.

learn: Multiplication is repeated groups. You can multiply a large number by a one-digit number by breaking it into place values. 4 × 312 = 4 × 300 + 4 × 10 + 4 × 2 = 1,200 + 40 + 8 = 1,248.
An area model draws a rectangle split into parts for each place value. You multiply each part and add the partial products.
To multiply two 2-digit numbers, like 23 × 14, find four partial products: 20 × 10 = 200, 20 × 4 = 80, 3 × 10 = 30, 3 × 4 = 12. Add: 200 + 80 + 30 + 12 = 322.
Multiplying by 10 adds one zero to a whole number: 45 × 10 = 450. Multiplying by 100 adds two zeros.
Division splits a number into equal groups. In 84 ÷ 4 = 21, 84 is the dividend, 4 is the divisor and 21 is the quotient.
Sometimes things do not divide evenly. The amount left over is the remainder. 17 ÷ 5 = 3 R2 because 5 × 3 = 15 and 2 are left.
To divide larger numbers, work from the left: divide, multiply, subtract, bring down, and repeat. You can also use partial quotients, taking away easy groups like 10 groups at a time.
In word problems, think about the remainder. If 26 students ride in cars that hold 4, you need 7 cars, because 6 cars only hold 24.
units.try: Find 157 ÷ 6. 6 goes into 15 two times (12). 15 − 12 = 3. Bring down 7 to make 37. 6 goes into 37 six times (36). 37 − 36 = 1. Answer: 26 R1. Check: 6 × 26 + 1 = 157.
check: 29 people ride in vans that hold 6. How many vans are needed?

learn: Factors are numbers you multiply to get a product. The factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12. Factor pairs of 12: 1 × 12, 2 × 6, 3 × 4.
A multiple is the product of a number and a whole number. Multiples of 4 are 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 and so on.
A prime number has exactly two factors, 1 and itself, like 2, 3, 5, 7, 11 and 13. A composite number has more than two factors, like 4, 6, 9 and 15. The number 1 is neither.
A pattern follows a rule. In 3, 7, 11, 15 the rule is add 4. Notice that every number in this pattern is odd.
units.try: List all factors of 24 using factor pairs: 1 × 24, 2 × 12, 3 × 8, 4 × 6. Factors: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24. Is 24 prime or composite? Composite, because it has more than two factors.

learn: A fraction names part of a whole. The bottom number, the denominator, tells how many equal parts the whole has. The top number, the numerator, tells how many parts you have.
Equivalent fractions name the same amount. Multiply or divide the top and bottom by the same number: 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6 = 4/8.
To compare fractions with the same denominator, compare numerators: 5/8 > 3/8. With the same numerator, the smaller denominator is bigger: 1/3 > 1/5, because thirds are bigger pieces.
For other fractions, make common denominators or compare to a benchmark like 1/2. 3/8 is less than 1/2, and 5/6 is more than 1/2, so 3/8 < 5/6.
units.try: Compare 2/3 and 3/4. Use 12 as a common denominator. 2/3 = 8/12 (multiply top and bottom by 4). 3/4 = 9/12 (multiply by 3). 8/12 < 9/12, so 2/3 < 3/4.

learn: When fractions have the same denominator, add or subtract the numerators and keep the denominator. 2/7 + 3/7 = 5/7. 5/6 − 1/6 = 4/6.
A mixed number has a whole number and a fraction, like 2 1/4. To add mixed numbers, add the wholes and add the fractions. If the fraction is more than 1, regroup it into a whole.
You can change a mixed number to an improper fraction: 2 1/4 = 9/4, because 2 wholes are 8 fourths plus 1 fourth.
To multiply a fraction by a whole number, multiply the numerator: 3 × 2/5 = 6/5 = 1 1/5. This is like adding 2/5 three times.
units.try: Find 1 3/8 + 2 7/8. Wholes: 1 + 2 = 3. Fractions: 3/8 + 7/8 = 10/8 = 1 2/8. Total: 3 + 1 2/8 = 4 2/8, which also equals 4 1/4.

learn: Decimals are another way to write fractions with denominators of 10 or 100. 3/10 = 0.3 (three tenths). 45/100 = 0.45 (forty-five hundredths).
The decimal point separates the whole number from the parts. In 2.75, the 2 is ones, the 7 is tenths and the 5 is hundredths.
Tenths and hundredths are related: 0.5 = 0.50, because 5 tenths equals 50 hundredths. So 3/10 + 4/100 = 30/100 + 4/100 = 34/100 = 0.34.

To compare decimals, line up the decimal points and compare from left to right. 0.6 > 0.58 because 6 tenths is more than 5 tenths. Money uses decimals: $1.25 is 1 dollar and 25 hundredths of a dollar.
units.try: Write 7/10 + 9/100 as a decimal. Change 7/10 to 70/100. Add: 70/100 + 9/100 = 79/100. As a decimal: 0.79.
check: How is 6/100 written as a decimal?

learn: Bigger units hold more small units. 1 foot = 12 inches, 1 yard = 3 feet, 1 pound = 16 ounces, 1 gallon = 4 quarts, 1 hour = 60 minutes. In metric: 1 meter = 100 centimeters, 1 kilometer = 1,000 meters, 1 kilogram = 1,000 grams, 1 liter = 1,000 milliliters.
To change a larger unit to a smaller one, multiply. 5 feet = 5 × 12 = 60 inches.
Perimeter is the distance around a shape. For a rectangle, add all sides or use P = 2 × length + 2 × width.
Area is the space inside a shape, measured in square units. For a rectangle, A = length × width. A room 8 feet by 10 feet has an area of 80 square feet.
units.try: A garden is 9 meters long and 4 meters wide. Perimeter: 2 × 9 + 2 × 4 = 18 + 8 = 26 meters. Area: 9 × 4 = 36 square meters.
check: How many inches are in 3 feet?
What is the area of a rectangle 7 cm by 6 cm?

learn: A point is an exact location. A line goes on forever in both directions. A line segment has two endpoints. A ray has one endpoint and goes on forever in one direction.

An angle is made by two rays with the same endpoint. Angles are measured in degrees with a protractor. A right angle is exactly 90°. An acute angle is less than 90°. An obtuse angle is more than 90° but less than 180°. A straight angle is 180°.
Parallel lines never meet, like train tracks. Perpendicular lines meet to form right angles, like the corner of a page.
A line of symmetry folds a shape into two matching halves. A square has 4 lines of symmetry. Shapes can be sorted by their angles and sides, such as right triangles or parallelograms.
units.try: Look around your room. Find one example each of a right angle, parallel lines and perpendicular lines. (Examples: a book corner is a right angle; the top and bottom edges of a door are parallel; a table leg meets the floor at perpendicular lines.)

rooms.about: Grade 4 science explores energy, waves and light, how plant and animal bodies work, and how Earth's surface changes over time through weathering, erosion, earthquakes and volcanoes.

learn: Energy is the ability to make things move or change. A moving object has energy of motion, called kinetic energy. The faster an object moves, the more energy it has.
Stored energy is called potential energy. A stretched rubber band, a ball held up high and a battery all store energy that can be released later.
When objects collide, energy is transferred. A bowling ball moving fast knocks pins harder than a slow one. Some energy also changes into sound and heat during a collision.
Energy is never used up or destroyed. It changes from one form to another or moves from one object to another.
units.try: Roll a ball gently into a stack of plastic cups, then roll it faster. Which roll moves the cups more? Explain using the word energy. (The faster ball has more kinetic energy, so it transfers more energy to the cups.)

units.t: Energy Transfer: Heat, Light, Sound and Electricity
learn: Energy can travel from place to place in different ways. Heat moves from warmer objects to cooler ones, like from hot cocoa into your hands.
Light carries energy from the sun to Earth. Sound carries energy through vibrations in air, water or solids.
Electricity is energy that flows through a circuit. A circuit is a complete loop with a power source (like a battery), wires and a device (like a bulb). If the loop is broken, electricity stops.
Materials that let heat or electricity pass easily are conductors, such as metals. Materials that block them are insulators, such as rubber, plastic and wood.
units.try: Make a list of five things at home that change electrical energy into another form. (Examples: a lamp makes light, a speaker makes sound, a toaster makes heat, a fan makes motion, a TV makes light and sound.)
check: Which is a good conductor of electricity?
What does a circuit need to work?

learn: A wave is a repeating disturbance that carries energy from one place to another. Waves move energy, but the water or material itself mostly moves up and down, not along with the wave.
The highest point of a wave is the crest and the lowest is the trough. Amplitude is how tall a wave is from its middle. Bigger amplitude means more energy.
Wavelength is the distance from one crest to the next crest. Waves with short wavelengths are close together.
Sound travels in waves. A loud sound has a big amplitude. People use wave patterns to send information, like radio signals and messages in codes of beeps.
units.try: Tie a rope or jump rope to a chair leg. Shake the free end slowly, then quickly. Notice that fast shaking makes shorter wavelengths, and bigger shakes make bigger amplitude.
check: What is the top of a wave called?
A wave with bigger amplitude has…

learn: Light travels in straight lines. When it hits an object, it can be reflected (bounced off), absorbed (taken in) or passed through.
We see an object when light reflects off it and enters our eyes. Without light, we cannot see anything, which is why a room with no light is completely dark.
Inside the eye, the pupil lets light in, the lens focuses it, and the retina at the back senses it. Nerves carry the signal to the brain, which makes the picture.
Mirrors reflect light well. Transparent materials like clear glass let light pass through. Opaque materials like wood block light and create shadows.
units.try: In a dim room, shine a flashlight at a mirror and try to bounce the light onto a target on the wall. You are showing that light travels in straight lines and reflects.
check: How do we see an object?
Light reflects off it into our eyes

learn: Living things have structures, or body parts, that help them survive, grow and reproduce. External structures are on the outside, and internal structures are on the inside.

Plants have roots to take in water and hold the plant in place, stems to carry water and food, leaves to make food from sunlight, and flowers that make seeds. Thorns can protect a plant from being eaten.
Animals have structures like shells for protection, claws and teeth for getting food, gills for breathing underwater and fur for warmth.
Inside, animals have organs such as a heart to pump blood, lungs to breathe and a stomach to digest food. Each organ has a job, and they work together.
units.try: Pick an animal, such as a turtle. List three of its structures and how each one helps it survive. (Sample: shell protects it, claws dig nests, beak tears food.)
check: Take in water and hold the plant

learn: Animals take in information through their senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch. Sense organs like eyes, ears, nose, tongue and skin have special receptors.
Nerves carry messages from the senses to the brain. The brain decides what to do and sends messages back to muscles.
Some reactions are very fast. If you touch a hot pan, you pull your hand back before you even think about it. This is called a reflex.
Different animals have special senses. Owls see well in the dark, dogs have a powerful sense of smell, and bats use echoes to find insects.
units.try: Ask a family member to drop a ruler between your open thumb and finger, and catch it as fast as you can. Note the centimeter mark. Try three times. Your eyes see it fall, your brain sends a signal, and your fingers react.
check: What carries messages from the senses to the brain?
A quick, automatic reaction is a…

learn: Weathering is the breaking down of rock into smaller pieces. Water, ice, wind, plant roots and chemicals can all cause weathering.
In ice wedging, water seeps into cracks, freezes and expands, and pushes the rock apart. Over many years, this can split huge boulders.
Erosion is the moving of weathered pieces, like sand and soil, by water, wind, ice or gravity. Deposition is when those pieces are dropped in a new place.
Rivers carve canyons over millions of years. The Grand Canyon was carved mainly by the Colorado River. Planting grass and trees helps hold soil and slow erosion.
units.try: Make a small hill of sand or dirt on a tray outdoors. Pour water slowly from a cup at the top. Watch where the soil moves and where it gets dropped. You have shown erosion and deposition.
check: Moving rock pieces to a new place

learn: Over a long time, layers of sediment such as sand and mud pile up and press into rock. These are called sedimentary rock layers.
In undisturbed layers, the bottom layers are oldest and the top layers are youngest.
Fossils are the remains or traces of living things from long ago, such as bones, shells, leaf prints or footprints, preserved in rock.
Fossils tell us how places have changed. Finding fish fossils on a mountain shows that the land was once under water.
units.try: Stack five colors of modeling clay or paper as layers. Label the bottom one 'oldest' and the top one 'youngest.' Hide a small shell between two layers and explain what that fossil's position says about its age.
check: In rock layers, where are the oldest layers usually found?
What do seashell fossils on a mountain suggest?
The area was once under water

learn: Earth's outer layer, the crust, is broken into giant pieces called plates that move very slowly, a few centimeters each year.
Earthquakes happen when plates suddenly slip, shaking the ground. Volcanoes are openings where melted rock called magma rises. Once it reaches the surface it is called lava.
Many earthquakes and volcanoes happen along plate edges. A large ring of them around the Pacific Ocean is called the Ring of Fire.
Maps show patterns of mountains, ocean trenches, earthquakes and volcanoes. Scientists use them to warn people and help keep communities safe.
units.try: Make an earthquake safety plan: In an earthquake, Drop to your hands and knees, take Cover under a sturdy table, and Hold On. Practice it once with your family.
check: What should you do in an earthquake?

learn: Natural resources are materials from Earth that people use, such as water, soil, wood, minerals and fuels.
Renewable resources can be replaced naturally in a short time, like sunlight, wind, flowing water and trees. Nonrenewable resources take millions of years to form, like coal, oil and natural gas.
Burning fossil fuels gives energy but also causes air pollution. Solar panels and wind turbines make electricity without burning fuel, but they depend on the weather.
We can conserve resources by reducing waste, reusing items and recycling materials.
units.try: Walk through your home and find three ways to save energy, such as turning off lights in empty rooms, unplugging chargers, or taking shorter showers. Write them on a note for your family.

rooms.about: Grade 4 social studies explores the regions of the United States, the Native nations who lived here first, how states grew, how state governments work, and what it means to be a good citizen.

learn: Geography is the study of Earth's places and people. Maps use a title, a key (or legend) to explain symbols, a compass rose to show directions, and a scale to show distance.
Lines of latitude run east and west and measure distance north or south of the equator. Lines of longitude run north and south and measure distance east or west of the prime meridian.
Together, latitude and longitude form a grid that gives every place an exact address, like 40° N, 74° W for New York City.
Physical maps show landforms like mountains, rivers and plains. Political maps show borders, states and cities.
units.try: Draw a map of your bedroom or yard. Include a title, a compass rose, a key with at least three symbols, and a simple scale such as 1 inch = 2 feet.
check: What does a map key show?
In circles around the poles only

learn: A region is an area with shared features. The United States is often divided into five regions: the Northeast, Southeast, Midwest, Southwest and West.

The Northeast has old cities, rocky coasts and forests. The Southeast has warm weather, farms and long coastlines. The Midwest has flat plains and rich soil and grows much of the nation's corn and wheat.
The Southwest has deserts, canyons and hot, dry weather. The West has tall mountains like the Rockies, the Pacific coast, and the states of Alaska and Hawaii.
Each region's land and climate affect how people live, what jobs they do and what foods they grow.
units.try: Find your state on a US map. Which region is it in? List two landforms and one crop or product from your region.
check: Which region is known for flat plains and corn?
The Rocky Mountains are in which region?

learn: Native Americans lived in North America for thousands of years before Europeans arrived. There were hundreds of nations, each with its own language, government and way of life.
People adapted to their environments. The Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) of the Northeast farmed corn, beans and squash, called the Three Sisters. Plains nations like the Lakota followed the buffalo.
In the Southwest, the Pueblo peoples built adobe homes and farmed in a dry land. In the Pacific Northwest, nations like the Tlingit fished for salmon and carved cedar.
Native nations are still here today. There are more than 570 federally recognized tribes in the United States, with their own governments.
units.try: Find out which Native nation or nations lived where your town is now. Write two facts about how they lived and one fact about them today.
check: What were the Three Sisters crops?
Are Native nations still part of the US today?
Yes, hundreds have their own governments

learn: In the 1400s and 1500s, European explorers sailed west looking for trade routes, gold and land. In 1492, Christopher Columbus reached islands in the Caribbean.

Spain, France, England and the Netherlands claimed land in the Americas. Spain built missions in the Southwest and Florida. France traded furs along rivers. England started colonies on the east coast.
Contact changed Native nations forever. Europeans brought diseases like smallpox that killed huge numbers of Native people, and they often took land by force.
In 1619, the first enslaved Africans were brought to the Virginia colony. Slavery would shape American history for over 240 years.
units.try: Make a two-column chart titled Explorers' Goals. On the left list what explorers wanted. On the right list how their arrival affected Native people.
check: Why did many European explorers sail west?
To find trade routes and riches
What caused many Native deaths after contact?

learn: The United States began with 13 states along the Atlantic coast. Over time, the country gained more land through purchases, treaties and wars.
The Louisiana Purchase in 1803 doubled the size of the country. Later the US gained Texas, the Southwest and the Pacific Northwest.
To become a state, a territory needed enough people and a written state constitution, and Congress had to approve. Hawaii became the 50th state in 1959.
This growth meant new homes for settlers but great loss for Native nations, who were often forced off their lands.
units.try: Find out when your state joined the United States and what number state it was. Write one sentence about who lived there before statehood.
check: How many states are in the United States today?
What did the Louisiana Purchase do?
Doubled the size of the country

learn: Each state has its own government with three branches, like the national government. The legislative branch makes laws, the executive branch carries out laws, and the judicial branch decides what laws mean.
A state's leader is the governor. The state legislature is made of elected lawmakers. Each state also has a constitution and a capital city.
Local governments run counties, cities and towns. A mayor or city council handles things like parks, police, fire departments, libraries and trash pickup.
Governments get money from taxes, which pay for schools, roads and other services people share.
units.try: Find the name of your state's governor and capital city, and your town or city's leader. Write down one service your local government provides.
check: Who leads a state's executive branch?

learn: Economics is about how people make, buy and sell goods and services. Goods are things you can touch, like apples. Services are jobs done for others, like haircuts.
Producers make goods or provide services. Consumers buy and use them. Most people are both.
Resources used to make things are natural resources (like trees), human resources (workers) and capital resources (tools and machines).
Regions specialize in what they do well and trade with others. Because people cannot have everything, they make choices. What you give up when you choose is called the opportunity cost.
units.try: You have $10 and want both a $10 book and a $10 game. Choose one. What is your opportunity cost? (Answer: the item you did not choose.)
check: What you give up when you choose

learn: Migration is moving from one place to another. People move for push factors, like war, hunger or few jobs, and pull factors, like jobs, freedom or family.
Immigrants are people who move to a new country to live. Millions came to the United States through places like Ellis Island in New York and Angel Island in California.
Not everyone came by choice. Millions of Africans were brought by force and enslaved.
Within the US, the Great Migration saw about 6 million Black Americans move from the South to Northern and Western cities between about 1910 and 1970, seeking jobs and escaping unfair laws.
units.try: Interview a family member or neighbor: Where did your family come from? Why did they move? Write two push factors or pull factors you heard.
check: Good jobs in a new place
Where did many immigrants arrive in New York?

learn: In the 1800s, new inventions changed how Americans lived and worked. Steam engines powered trains and factories.

The transcontinental railroad was finished in 1869. It linked the East and West coasts and cut a months-long trip down to about a week. Many Chinese and Irish immigrants did the hard, dangerous work of building it.
The telegraph sent messages over wires in minutes. Later, the telephone and electric light bulb changed homes and businesses.
Factories grew in cities, and many workers, including children, worked long hours in unsafe conditions. Over time, laws were passed to protect workers.
units.try: Make a timeline with three inventions: telegraph (1840s), transcontinental railroad (1869), telephone (1876). Next to each, write how it changed daily life.
check: When was the transcontinental railroad finished?

learn: A citizen is a member of a community or country. Citizens have rights, like freedom of speech, and responsibilities, like obeying laws and respecting others.
Good citizens help their communities. They vote when they are adults, serve on juries, volunteer and stay informed about issues.
Kids can be good citizens too: picking up litter, helping neighbors, following school rules and treating others fairly.
People can change things peacefully by writing letters to leaders, speaking at meetings, signing petitions and voting.
units.try: Find a small problem in your neighborhood or school, such as litter in a park. Write a short, polite letter to a local leader explaining the problem and one idea to fix it.
check: Which is a responsibility of citizens?
How can people change a rule peacefully?

rooms.about: Grade 4 art builds drawing, painting, printmaking and sculpture skills while learning the elements of art, color, perspective and how to talk thoughtfully about artworks from many cultures.

learn: The elements of art are the building blocks artists use: line, shape, form, color, value, texture and space.
Line is a mark that moves through space. Shape is a flat area, like a circle or square. Form is three-dimensional, like a sphere or cube, with height, width and depth.
Value is how light or dark a color is. Texture is how something feels or looks like it would feel, such as rough, smooth or fuzzy.
Space is the area around and between things. Positive space is the object itself, and negative space is the empty area around it.
units.try: Fold a paper into eight boxes. In seven boxes draw a quick example of each element: line, shape, form, color, value, texture and space. In the last box, make a tiny picture that uses them all.
check: How light or dark a color is

learn: The primary colors are red, yellow and blue. Mixing two primaries makes a secondary color: red + yellow = orange, yellow + blue = green, blue + red = violet.
A color wheel arranges colors in a circle. Complementary colors sit opposite each other, like red and green or blue and orange. Placed side by side, they look bold and bright.
Warm colors (red, orange, yellow) feel energetic or hot. Cool colors (blue, green, violet) feel calm or cold.
Adding white to a color makes a tint (lighter). Adding black makes a shade (darker).
units.try: With paints, crayons or markers, make your own color wheel with six colors. Then paint one small square with a tint of blue and one with a shade of blue.
check: What do yellow and blue make?
What is the complement of orange?

learn: Shading uses value to make flat drawings look three-dimensional. Light hits one side of an object, called the highlight, and the opposite side is in shadow.
A value scale shows steps from white to black. Practice by pressing lightly for light values and harder for dark ones.
Shading techniques include blending (smooth gray), hatching (parallel lines), cross-hatching (crossing lines) and stippling (dots). The closer the lines or dots, the darker it looks.
A cast shadow is the shadow an object throws onto the table or ground, on the side away from the light.
units.try: Draw a circle. Pick a light direction, such as the top left. Leave a small white highlight there, then shade gradually darker toward the bottom right. Add a cast shadow on the ground. Your circle becomes a ball.
check: Where is the highlight on an object?

learn: Artists show depth on flat paper with tricks called perspective. The foreground is closest to the viewer, the middle ground is in the middle, and the background is farthest away.
Objects that are far away look smaller and are placed higher on the page. Objects that are close look bigger and are placed lower.
Overlapping, putting one object in front of another, shows which is closer.
Faraway things look paler and less detailed, while close things have strong color and clear details.
units.try: Draw a landscape with three trees: a big, detailed tree low in the foreground, a medium tree in the middle ground, and a small, pale tree high in the background. Overlap some hills behind them.
check: Which part of a picture is closest to the viewer?

learn: A portrait is an artwork of a person. A self-portrait is one the artist makes of himself or herself.
Proportion is how sizes of parts relate to each other. On most faces, the eyes are about halfway between the top of the head and the chin.
The bottom of the nose is about halfway between the eyes and the chin, and the mouth is a little below the nose. The ears line up from the eyes to the bottom of the nose.
Portraits can also show personality through expression, clothing, background and color.
units.try: Look in a mirror and draw an egg shape for your head. Draw a light line halfway down for your eyes. Add your nose, mouth and ears using the proportion guides. Then add your hair and a background that shows something you love.
check: Where are the eyes on most faces?
Art an artist makes of himself or herself

learn: A landscape is an artwork showing natural scenery, such as mountains, fields, rivers or skies. A seascape shows the sea, and a cityscape shows buildings.
The horizon line is where the sky seems to meet the land or water. Placing it low gives more sky; placing it high gives more land.
Artists choose colors and brushstrokes to show mood and weather. Short dabs can show sparkling light; long smooth strokes can show calm water.
Many artists paint outdoors to study real light, which changes through the day.
units.try: Look out a window or sit outside. Draw the horizon line first, then fill in the sky, land and one detail. Use warm colors for a sunny mood or cool colors for a calm or chilly mood.
check: Where sky seems to meet land
A picture of city buildings is a…

learn: Printmaking is making an image that can be copied many times. The artist creates a printing plate, rolls ink onto it, and presses paper on top.
In relief printing, the raised parts of the plate get the ink. Anything carved away stays the paper's color.
A print comes out as a mirror image, so letters must be carved backward.
Each copy is called a print or an impression. Artists number them, such as 3/10, meaning the third print of ten.
units.try: Press a design into a clean foam tray with a dull pencil. Roll or brush washable paint over it, press paper on top and rub gently. Peel it off and see your print. Make two more prints in different colors.
check: In relief printing, which part gets ink?
Why must letters be carved backward?
Prints come out as mirror images

learn: A sculpture is three-dimensional art you can walk around. Sculptures can be made of clay, stone, wood, metal, paper or found objects.
Additive sculpture means building up by adding material, like joining clay coils. Subtractive sculpture means taking material away, like carving soap or stone.
Clay hand-building methods include the pinch pot (pressing a ball into a bowl shape), coil building (stacking ropes of clay) and slab building (using flat sheets).
To join clay pieces, score (scratch) both surfaces, add slip (watery clay) and press them together.
units.try: Using play clay or salt dough, make a pinch pot. Roll a ball the size of an orange, push your thumb into the middle, and pinch the walls evenly while turning it. Add a small coil handle using score and slip.
check: Carving soap is an example of…

learn: People everywhere make art to celebrate, remember, decorate and tell stories. Learning about art from many cultures helps us understand one another.
In Mexico, papel picado is colorful tissue paper cut into lacy designs for celebrations. In West Africa, kente cloth is woven in bright patterns where colors and shapes have meanings.
Aboriginal Australian artists have used dots, lines and symbols to tell stories about land and ancestors for thousands of years. Japanese artists made famous woodblock prints of waves and mountains.
When we learn from another culture's art, we show respect by learning its meaning and giving credit, rather than copying sacred designs.
units.try: Fold tissue paper or thin paper several times and cut small shapes along the folds to make a papel picado style banner. Open it up to see the repeating pattern.
check: Papel picado comes from which country?
How do we show respect for another culture's art?
Learn its meaning and give credit

units.t: Looking at and Talking About Art
learn: Art critics follow four steps. Describe: tell what you see. Analyze: explain how the elements and principles are used.
Interpret: decide what the artwork means or what mood it creates. Judge: share your opinion and give reasons.
Use art words: This painting uses warm colors and curved lines that make me feel happy. Avoid just saying I like it or I don't like it.
Respect other people's art. When giving feedback, start with something that works, then offer a kind suggestion.
units.try: Choose any picture in a book or poster at home. Write one sentence for each step: describe, analyze, interpret and judge.
check: Which is the first step of art criticism?
Which is a helpful art comment?
The bright colors make it feel joyful

rooms.about: Grade 4 music grows your skills in reading rhythms and notes on the treble staff, singing in harmony, playing simple melodies, and recognizing instruments, musical forms and American musical traditions.

learn: The beat is the steady pulse of music, like a heartbeat. Rhythm is the pattern of long and short sounds that goes over the beat.
A quarter note gets 1 beat. A half note gets 2 beats. A whole note gets 4 beats. Two eighth notes share 1 beat, and four sixteenth notes share 1 beat.
Rests are beats of silence. A quarter rest is 1 silent beat, a half rest is 2 and a whole rest is a whole measure of silence.
Musicians often count rhythms with words: ta for a quarter note, ti-ti for two eighths, and ti-ka-ti-ka for four sixteenths.
units.try: Pat a steady beat on your knees. Clap this pattern while saying the syllables: ta, ti-ti, ti-ka-ti-ka, ta. Repeat it four times without stopping the beat.
check: How many beats does a half note get?
How many sixteenth notes fit in one beat?

learn: Music is divided into measures by bar lines. Each measure has the same number of beats.
The time signature at the start of the music has two numbers. The top number tells how many beats are in a measure. The bottom number tells which note gets one beat; a 4 means the quarter note.
In 4/4 time there are four beats per measure; it is so common it is called common time. In 3/4 there are three beats, used for waltzes. In 2/4 there are two beats, used for marches.
The first beat of each measure is usually the strongest, called the downbeat.
units.try: Conduct in 3/4 time: move your hand down on beat 1, out to the side on beat 2 and up on beat 3. Count 1-2-3 while humming a waltz.
check: In 3/4 time, how many beats are in a measure?

units.t: Reading Notes on the Treble Staff
learn: Music is written on a staff of five lines and four spaces. The treble clef, also called the G clef, curls around the second line, which is the note G.
The notes on the lines from bottom to top are E, G, B, D, F. A saying to remember them is Every Good Boy Does Fine.
The notes in the spaces from bottom to top spell the word FACE.
Notes higher on the staff sound higher in pitch. Middle C sits on a short extra line below the staff, called a ledger line.
units.try: Draw a staff with five lines. Write a whole note in each space and label it F, A, C, E. Then write notes on the lines and label them E, G, B, D, F.
check: What do the treble staff spaces spell?
The treble clef is also called…

learn: Dynamics are how loud or soft music is. Musicians use Italian words: piano (p) means soft, forte (f) means loud, mezzo piano (mp) means medium soft and mezzo forte (mf) means medium loud.
Crescendo means gradually getting louder. Decrescendo or diminuendo means gradually getting softer.
Tempo is the speed of the beat. Largo is very slow, andante is a walking pace, moderato is medium, and allegro is fast and lively.
Composers choose dynamics and tempo to create mood. A soft, slow lullaby feels calm; a loud, fast march feels exciting.
units.try: Sing a song you know four ways: piano and slow, forte and slow, piano and fast, forte and fast. Which version fits the song best? Why?

learn: Form is the plan or structure of a piece of music. Musicians label sections with letters. Sections that are the same get the same letter.
AB form, called binary, has two different sections. ABA form, called ternary, has a section, a different section, then the first section returns.
Rondo form returns to the A section again and again with different sections in between: ABACA.
Many songs use verse and chorus. Verses usually have different words each time, while the chorus repeats the same words.
units.try: Listen to a favorite song. Each time the chorus comes back, raise your hand. Write the form using letters, such as A (verse), B (chorus), A, B.

learn: Instruments of the orchestra belong to four families. Strings (violin, viola, cello, double bass, harp) make sound when strings vibrate.

Woodwinds (flute, clarinet, oboe, bassoon) make sound when air vibrates in a tube, often with a reed. Brass (trumpet, trombone, French horn, tuba) make sound when players buzz their lips into a mouthpiece.
Percussion instruments (drums, xylophone, cymbals, triangle) are struck, shaken or scraped.
In each family, bigger instruments make lower sounds. The tuba is lower than the trumpet, and the cello is lower than the violin.
units.try: Stretch a rubber band around an open box and pluck it. Then tighten it or use a thinner band. Notice how the pitch changes. This is how string instruments work.
check: Which instrument is in the brass family?
In an instrument family, larger instruments sound…

learn: A melody is a series of notes that makes a tune. It is the part you hum after hearing a song.
Melodies move in steps (to the very next note, like line to space), skips (jumping over one note) and leaps (bigger jumps). Some notes repeat.
A melody's contour is its shape: it may go up, go down or stay the same. Drawing the contour as a line helps you see it.
Most melodies end on a home note called the tonic, which makes the music feel finished.
units.try: Sing the first line of a familiar song like Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star and trace the contour in the air with your finger. Where does it leap? Where does it step?
check: Moving from a line note to the very next space note is a…
The home note that makes music feel finished is the…

learn: Harmony happens when two or more different notes sound at the same time. It adds richness to music.
A round is a song where groups sing the same melody but start at different times, like Row, Row, Row Your Boat. The parts overlap and make harmony.
Partner songs are two different songs that can be sung at the same time and sound good together.
A chord is three or more notes played together. Guitars and pianos often play chords to accompany a melody.
units.try: With a family member, sing Row, Row, Row Your Boat as a round. One person starts; the second begins when the first reaches 'gently down the stream.' Keep your part steady.
check: The same melody started at different times
Three or more notes played together

learn: The recorder is a simple woodwind instrument. Hold it with your left hand on top and your right hand on the bottom. Your left thumb covers the hole on the back.
Blow gently, as if cooling soup, and say doo with your tongue to start each note. Blowing too hard makes a squeak.
The first notes most students learn are B (thumb and first finger), A (add the second finger) and G (add the third finger).
With just B, A and G, you can play melodies like Hot Cross Buns: B A G, B A G, G G G G A A A A, B A G.
units.try: If you have a recorder, play Hot Cross Buns slowly. If not, practice the fingerings on a pencil and sing the note names: B A G, B A G.
check: Which hand goes on top of the recorder?
What happens if you blow too hard?

learn: Folk songs are passed down from person to person and often tell about work, travel or everyday life. Many have no known composer.
Spirituals are songs created by enslaved African Americans. They expressed faith, sorrow and hope, and some may have carried hidden messages about escape.
Jazz began in New Orleans in the early 1900s. It mixes African and European traditions and uses improvisation, which means making up music on the spot. Louis Armstrong was a famous jazz trumpeter.
Blues, country, gospel, rock and hip-hop also grew in America, and each built on earlier styles.
units.try: Clap a steady beat and make up your own four-beat rhythm on the spot, then a different one. You are improvising, like a jazz musician.
check: Making up music on the spot

rooms.about: Grade 4 Health & PE builds fitness and movement skills, teamwork and sportsmanship, and healthy habits for eating, hygiene, safety and handling feelings.

learn: Physical fitness means your body can do daily tasks and play with energy. It has five main parts.
Cardiovascular endurance is how well your heart and lungs work during long activity, like running or swimming. Muscular strength is how much force your muscles can make, like lifting.
Muscular endurance is how long muscles can keep working, like doing many sit-ups. Flexibility is how far your joints can move, like reaching your toes.
Body composition is the balance of muscle, bone, fat and water in your body. Kids should be active for at least 60 minutes every day.
units.try: Do a mini fitness check: count how many jumping jacks you can do in 30 seconds (endurance), how long you can hold a wall sit (muscular endurance), and how far you can reach toward your toes while sitting (flexibility). Write your results to compare later.
check: How many minutes a day should kids be active?

learn: A warm-up gets your body ready to move. It raises your heart rate and warms your muscles so they are less likely to get hurt. Try 5 minutes of easy moves like marching, arm circles and slow jogging.
A cool-down lets your heart rate slow gradually after exercise. Walk slowly and breathe deeply for a few minutes.
Stretching improves flexibility. Hold each stretch gently for about 15 to 30 seconds. Never bounce, and stop if it hurts.
Drink water before, during and after exercise, especially on hot days.
units.try: Do a five-move warm-up at home in a safe open space: 30 seconds each of marching, arm circles, side steps, gentle knee lifts and slow jumping jacks. Then hold a calf stretch and a shoulder stretch for 20 seconds each.
check: To get muscles ready and prevent injury
Bounce as hard as you can

learn: Your heart is a muscle about the size of your fist. It pumps blood carrying oxygen to your whole body.
Your pulse is the beat you feel as blood is pushed through your arteries. You can find it on the thumb side of your wrist or on the side of your neck.
A resting heart rate for kids is often about 70 to 110 beats per minute. During exercise it goes up to deliver more oxygen to your muscles.
Regular exercise makes your heart stronger, so it can pump more blood with each beat.
units.try: Find your pulse with two fingers (not your thumb). Count beats for 15 seconds and multiply by 4. Then do jumping jacks for 1 minute and check again. Compare the two numbers.
check: Where can you find your pulse?
What happens to your heart rate during exercise?

learn: Locomotor skills move you from place to place: walking, running, skipping, galloping, hopping, leaping and sliding.
To throw overhand, stand sideways to your target, step with the opposite foot, bring your arm back, and follow through toward the target.
To catch, watch the ball, reach out with your hands, and pull the ball in toward your body to soften the catch.
Dribbling a basketball uses your fingertips, not your palm. Keep the ball at waist height and look up instead of at the ball.
units.try: With a soft ball, practice ten overhand throws to a wall target, stepping with the opposite foot each time. Then practice ten catches, pulling the ball in toward your body.
check: When throwing overhand, which foot steps forward?
The foot opposite your throwing arm
The foot on the same side
When dribbling a basketball, use your…

learn: Sportsmanship means playing fair and treating others with respect, whether you win or lose.
Good sports follow the rules, take turns, encourage teammates, accept the referee's calls, and shake hands or say good game at the end.
Teamwork means working together toward a goal. Teammates communicate, share the ball and support each other after mistakes.
Everyone makes mistakes when learning a skill. Saying nice try or you'll get it next time helps the whole team improve.
units.try: Play a simple game at home with family, like tossing a ball into a basket. Practice saying one encouraging thing every turn, and say good game at the end no matter who wins.
check: What should you say after a teammate makes a mistake?

learn: A healthy plate has five food groups: fruits, vegetables, grains, protein and dairy. Each group gives your body different nutrients.
Try to fill half your plate with fruits and vegetables. Grains, like brown rice and whole-wheat bread, give energy. At least half your grains should be whole grains.
Protein foods, like beans, eggs, fish, chicken and nuts, help build muscles. Dairy foods, like milk, yogurt and cheese, help build strong bones and teeth.
Foods with lots of added sugar, salt or fat, like candy and chips, are fine sometimes but should not replace healthy foods.
units.try: Draw a plate and divide it into the five food groups. Plan a dinner with one food from each group. (Sample: grilled chicken, brown rice, broccoli, apple slices and a glass of milk.)
check: How much of your plate should be fruits and vegetables?
Which food group helps build strong bones?

learn: Your body is more than half water. You need water to keep cool, digest food and think clearly. Drink water throughout the day, and more when it is hot or you are active.
Many sodas and sports drinks have lots of added sugar. One can of soda can have about 10 teaspoons of sugar.
A Nutrition Facts label tells the serving size, calories and nutrients in a food. Check the serving size first, because the numbers are for one serving.
Look for foods higher in fiber and lower in added sugars and sodium (salt).
units.try: Find a Nutrition Facts label at home. Write down the serving size, calories per serving and grams of added sugar. If you ate two servings, how much sugar would that be? (Double the number.)
check: What is the best drink for thirst most of the time?
What should you check first on a food label?

learn: Germs are tiny living things, like bacteria and viruses, that can make you sick. They spread through touching, coughing and sneezing.
Wash your hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds, especially before eating and after using the bathroom. Cough or sneeze into your elbow.
Brush your teeth twice a day for two minutes and floss daily. Bathe regularly and wear clean clothes.
As you grow, your body changes. You may sweat more, so using deodorant and showering after exercise helps you stay fresh. Everyone grows on their own schedule.
units.try: Time yourself washing your hands while humming Happy Birthday twice (about 20 seconds). Scrub palms, backs, between fingers, thumbs and under nails.
check: How long should you wash your hands?
Where should you cough or sneeze?

learn: Always wear a helmet that fits when riding a bike, scooter or skateboard. Ride on the right side of the road, with traffic, and use hand signals.
Around water, swim only with an adult watching, and never dive into shallow water. Wear a life jacket on boats.
For fire safety, know two ways out of every room and a family meeting spot outside. If there is smoke, stay low and get out. Stop, drop and roll if your clothes catch fire.
Online, never share your full name, address, school or passwords. Tell a trusted adult if anything online makes you uncomfortable. Call 911 only for real emergencies.
units.try: Draw a map of your home with two escape routes from your bedroom and mark your family's outdoor meeting spot. Practice the route with your family.
check: What should you do if your clothes catch fire?
Which is safe to share online?

learn: Everyone has feelings, like happy, sad, angry, nervous and excited. All feelings are normal. What matters is how we handle them.
Stress is how your body reacts to pressure, like a big test. Healthy ways to cope include deep breathing, exercise, talking to someone and getting enough sleep, about 9 to 12 hours for kids your age.
Bullying is when someone hurts another person on purpose, again and again. It can be hitting, name-calling, leaving people out or being mean online.
If you see bullying, don't join in. Stand with the person being hurt and tell a trusted adult. Kindness, like including others, makes everyone feel safer.
units.try: Practice box breathing: breathe in for 4 counts, hold for 4, breathe out for 4, hold for 4. Repeat four times. Use it next time you feel nervous or upset.
check: What should you do if you see bullying?
Which is a healthy way to handle stress?
